results.original: An artificial intelligence tutor answers questions about a collection of course documents. The tutor uses a language model to generate explanations, but fluent wording does not guarantee factual accuracy. During training, the language model adjusts its parameters using examples from a training dataset. A separate validation dataset supports model selection and the choice of training settings. A held-out test dataset measures performance after those choices have been made. These datasets must be separated carefully: if passages from the same source appear in both training and testing, the measured performance can overstate the model's ability to handle unfamiliar material. Dataset size alone does not establish dataset quality.

results.original: The tutor's language model uses a decoder-only transformer to process text. A tokenizer divides an input passage into tokens, and an embedding layer maps those tokens to numerical vectors. Positional information helps the transformer distinguish sequences containing the same tokens in different orders. In each attention layer, self-attention combines information from token representations. A causal attention mask prevents a position from attending to later positions when the model predicts the next token. This restriction applies during both training and generation. Attention can connect information across a passage, but the model's finite context window limits the amount of text available in a single request. An attention weight does not establish that the associated claim is true.

results.original: Training compares the model's predicted token probabilities with the next tokens in the training examples. A loss function measures prediction error, and backpropagation computes gradients used by an optimizer to update model parameters. The learning rate controls the size of those updates. A learning rate that is too large can make training unstable, whereas a very small learning rate can slow improvement. Overfitting occurs when improved training performance fails to translate into performance on unseen examples. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly disables some activations during training; ordinary inference uses the trained network without that random disabling. Early stopping uses validation performance to decide when to end training, rather than selecting a stopping point using the held-out test results.
results.reconstruction: Training compares models predicted token probabilities with next tokens in the training examples. A loss function quantifies error metric of prediction error. Backpropagation computes gradients, which are used by an optimizer to update model parameters. The learning rate controls size of updates of those updates; it can make unstable training stability when learning rate is too large and can slows improvement speed when learning rate is very small. Overfitting occurs when improved training performance fails to translate into performance on unseen examples. Dropout randomly disables some activations during training. Ordinary inference employs trained network for operation without that random disabling. Early stopping uses metric to guide action using validation performance to decide when to end training and does not use held out test results for selecting a stopping point.

results.original: After training, the tutor uses quantization and retrieval-augmented generation for different purposes. Weight quantization stores model parameters with fewer bits, reducing the memory required to store those parameters, although an aggressive reduction in precision can degrade answer quality. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies relevant course passages when the tutor answers a question. A retrieval encoder maps the question and document passages into embeddings, and a similarity search selects candidate passages from an index. The selected passages are added to the language model's context. Updating this document index can make revised course material available without retraining the language model. Retrieval does not itself change the model's parameters, and a highly ranked passage can still be irrelevant, outdated, or incorrect.
results.reconstruction: The tutor employs weight quantization after training to store model parameters with fewer bits, thereby reducing the memory required to store those parameters. However, an aggressive reduction in precision may degrade answer quality. The tutor also employs retrieval augmented generation after training for different purposes; when the tutor answers a question, this technique supplies relevant course passages. A retrieval encoder maps inputs of the question and document passages into embeddings, which similarity search uses to select candidate passages from an index. These selected passages are added to language models context. A document index enables access to revised course material via updating and can allow avoidance of language model retraining for making revised course material available. Retrieval does not itself change models parameters. Even a highly ranked passage can still be irrelevant, outdated, or incorrect.
